The light on the estuary did not fall so much as settle, like silt through heavy water.

For forty years, Julian had kept the workshop at the bend where the river forgot its name and became the sea. It was a low-ceilinged room smelling of beeswax, whale oil, and the dry, iron tang of cut brass. The work he did had no modern name, though historically people had called it many things: horology, instrument-making, or simply *repair*. But Julian did not repair clocks that told the hour of trains or shifts at the textile mill. He worked on things that measured what people could neither spend nor recover.

On his workbench lay an anemometer from an 18th-century survey brig, its four silver cups tarnished to the color of wet slate. Beside it sat a cedar-wood box containing thirty-two numbered vials of sand, each gathered from a different latitude along the African coast, labeled in an ink that had faded from gall-black to the color of dried tea. 

The bell above the heavy oak door did not ring; it clicked, a brass counterweight shifting against a lead pin. 

Julian did not look up immediately. He was seating a hair-spring into the balance wheel of a pocket instrument meant to gauge the density of mountain fog. His fingers were long, the skin across his knuckles paper-thin and cross-hatched with pale silver scars where screwdrivers had slipped over the decades.

"The tide is out," the visitor said.

The voice was thin, dry, and carried the flat vowels of the inland plains. Julian set down his loupe, blinking against the sudden rush of unfiltered gray light from the north-facing window.

The man standing near the threshold was young, though he wore an overcoat that had belonged to someone broader and older. His boots were dusted with dry, chalky clay from the upper ridges. In his hands, wrapped in a square of oilcloth tied with hemp twine, he held a bundle the size of a loaf of bread.

"It doesn't turn," the young man said. "My grandfather told me that if it stopped turning, the soil under the orchard would go sour. It stopped three days after the Michaelmas frost."

"Set it on the felt," Julian said.

The young man approached with the cautious, unbalanced gait of someone carrying unexploded ordnance. He laid the parcel upon the green baize of the central table and stepped back, his hands retreating deep into his oversized pockets.

Julian untied the twine. The knot had been tied with three half-hitches, tight and weathered, sealed with a dab of red candle wax. When the oilcloth fell away, it revealed a sphere of dark bell-metal, pierced through with hundreds of tiny, irregular apertures, like a dried poppy head magnified forty times. From its pole protruded a spindle of fluted steel, ending in a counter-weighted escapement made of polished bone.

"An aerophone," Julian murmured. "Or a vernacular variant of one."

"It has no gears," the boy said. "I shook it. Nothing rattles."

"You shouldn't have shaken it," Julian said mildly, picking up a camel-hair brush to sweep away the crumbs of dried mud clinging to the base. "It isn't a clockwork. It works by thermal convection and the barometric gradient between dawn and dusk. When the air pressure drops before rain, the mercury reservoir in the lower hemisphere expands through a porous diaphragm of boxwood. That turns the bone spindle, which sounds the internal reeds."

He leaned close, his breath fogging the dark metal. Through the tiny apertures, deep within the sphere, something faint and iridescent caught the daylight—a film of dried glycerin, or perhaps old varnish meant to keep the reeds from rusting.

"Can you make it breathe again?" the young man asked. His gaze wandered to the shelves: row upon row of glass bell-jars housing dead compasses, spirit levels filled with green elderberry wine, balance scales sensitive enough to weigh the graphite left behind by a signature.

"I can clean the diaphragm," Julian replied. "I can replace the gasket with cured pigskin. But whether it will sing for you depends on where you place it. These instruments were calibrated for stone houses with drafty floors and open hearths. If you take it back to a house with double-glazed windows and hot-water radiators, it will stay dumb. It requires an imperfection in the room to register the world."

The young man frowned, looking down at his boots. "The house is old enough. You can feel the wind through the wainscoting when the gale comes off the marsh."

"Then leave it. Come back when the moon changes."

"How much will it be?"

"Three pounds of beeswax and whatever you can spare of the dried lavender from last summer," Julian said. "The paraffin from the chemist is too greasy for the brass."

The young man nodded, seemingly relieved by a currency he understood, and turned toward the door. As he lifted the latch, he paused, his silhouette stark against the white, salt-glazed horizon outside.

"Did people really believe it?" he asked. "About the orchard?"

Julian picked up his tweezers and gently nudged the bone spindle. It gave a microscopic, shuddering creak, then fell silent.

"People used to believe that things had obligations to them," Julian said. "They thought a clock kept time out of loyalty, and that an iron hinge groaned because it shared the house's fatigue. It is not a very useful way to understand mechanics, but it made them take better care of their tools."

The door clicked shut. The counterweight swung twice, then settled.

Julian sat back down on his high stool. The estuary was draining out toward the shoals, leaving miles of glistening, ribbed mud that mirrored the sky until there was no horizon left, only a seamless sphere of pearl and slate. 

He did not immediately begin work on the boy's sphere. Instead, he reached for a small, unlabelled jar of almond oil and a square of chamois. He began to polish the edge of the workbench itself, smoothing the wood where thousands of hours of his own forearms had worn the beech down to a polish as slick and pale as ivory. 

Outside, a curlew cried—two rising notes, lonely and sharp as an awl—and then the tide turned, silent and heavy, pushing its cold, gray tongue back into the mouth of the land.
